URL: https://www.politico.eu/article/the-city-of-london-isnt-up-for-more-brexit-trauma/
Politico Europe, 16 November 2026 (FULL-TEXT via curl)

Andy Burnham has floated grand ideas about the U.K.’s future relationship with the EU. Britain’s finance powerhouses aren’t paying too much attention yet.

LONDON — Britain's financial powerhouse isn’t ready to take Andy Burnham seriously on Brexit.

Since becoming Britain's prime minister in July, Burnham has floated grander ideas about reshaping the U.K.'s relationship with the EU, or even rejoining the bloc, and will head to Brussels for a major summit this week to begin to reset relations.

But after a decade of political turmoil, the City of London's financial sector doesn’t want to hear it.

“We’re not going to be lobbying or aggravating or pushing it our side,” a banking lobbyist, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to speak freely.

“The City will be more quiet,” said a second finance lobbyist.

While the majority of the City backed Remain in the 2016 referendum on Britain's membership of the bloc, banks, insurers and money managers have spent years rewiring their businesses for life outside the EU.

After initially pushing lofty goals for its new relationship with the EU, the City was left out of the Brexit deal in 2020, and kept on the sidelines for years.

Even as relations thawed under former Conservative Prime Minister Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer’s Labour government, the U.K. financial services industry has played only a minimal role in the reset of relations.

Only U.K. clearinghouses, part of the plumbing wiring the financial system, maintain direct access to EU clients.

Instead, the City has been reshaping the U.K. finance rulebook to its liking, fashioning a new life for itself outside the bloc.

After being shut out of EU markets and disappointed by British politicians over the years, lobbyists representing all stripes of the financial services sector say they are firmly ignoring Burnham’s suggestion Britain could rekindle its relationship with the bloc.

The Labour leader has gone the furthest of any PM since the 2016 Brexit vote by saying he wants to see the U.K. rejoin the EU in his lifetime. He'll head to Brussels for the Nov. 20 summit where he is expected to sign off new agreements on agri-food trade, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme, and has opened up the possibility of rejoining the single market, customs union, or even the EU wholesale.

But the City has so far dismissed his suggestions of reentering the bloc as politicking, rather than a possibility they have to grapple with.

The discussion is “farfetched,” said a third lobbyist, whose job straddles both the EU and U.K., adding their company won't be engaging until Burnham’s proposals become more concrete.

“The political hurdles are pretty legitimate,” the same lobbyist said of rejoining. “What will the EU want to extract and will the U.K. accept?”

Since the referendum, many financial services firms have relocated vast sums of money and members of staff setting up offices on the continent to be able to continue serving EU customers.

“There’s a lot of sunk costs in what everybody has done to get business ready,” the lobbyist said.

And there’s little appetite to re-run the old debates or sit through more years of disruption — especially amid fears London could fall behind the U.S. in a technological revolution.

“It took several years to leave, it will take several years to re-enter,” said a City lawyer. “Can we afford that level of distraction?”

With the City broadly happy with a nimbler, streamlined rulebook, there is also a reluctance to enter back into the Brussels rule-making machine.

“In an ideal world, you’d have market access and your own rules, but that is not possible,” the lawyer said, referring to the red line to adopt EU rules to gain access to the single market.

It's a lesson the City learned the hard way after Brexit, when, despite having identical rulebooks, the EU didn't allow for “cherry-picking” by U.K. finance firms once they exited the bloc.

And despite the City's continued efforts, and a flagship deal with Switzerland that allows firms to operate in the Alpine nation while still following the U.K.’s regulatory rulebook, the EU isn't likely to budge on that principle.

Paulina Dejmek Hack, who was a top staffer for EU Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and involved in the negotiations with the U.K., is now the director general of the European Commission's financial-services department (DG FISMA), making her the key EU official for the City.

“She'll be very orthodox,” said a fourth lobbyist, with an EU-U.K. role. “She's not going to do a deal like that.”

Still, while the City may be wary of Burnham's words, and reluctant to engage early on, the huge economic prize of unfettered market access might ultimately outweigh the new Brexit rulebook.

“If it comes down to it, I don't think the City would come out strongly against rejoin,” the second lobbyist said.

There could be a tougher divide. While conversations within firms or associations are yet to happen in a serious way, the industry would likely split — potentially including within businesses — on the benefits.

“Parts of a business may be relying on a quirk to make more money, but more profitable parts of the business may want to rejoin,” the second lobbyist said.

“There won’t be consensus on what to do and there won’t be a huge appetite to jump back in,” added the banking lobbyist, who nevertheless said the industry should be ready if the Treasury comes knocking.

Thursday’s increase is unlikely to be the last unless Middle East conflict resolved, said Andrew Bailey.

Britain’s chancellor unveils first budget of the Andy Burnham era — as watchdog reveals decade-long pressure on living standards.

“Regulation is not, in my view, the right place to start,” Andrew Bailey said Wednesday.

The City of London is lobbying hard against the prospect of a windfall tax on the banks ahead of the October budget.
